name: אֲדֹנִי־צֶדֶק
gloss: lord of righteousness; or my lord is righteousness
summary: The king of Jerusalem when Israel entered the land. Hearing that Gibeon had made peace with Joshua, he called four other kings of the Amorites to attack it; Joshua defeated them at Gibeon, brought the five out of the cave at Makkedah, and put them to death. The name is אָדוֹן “lord” joined to צֶדֶק “righteousness” by ‑i, built exactly as the name of an earlier king of the same city, מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק king of Salem, which Hebrews translates “king of righteousness”: so “lord of righteousness”. Read with the i as “my”, it is a sentence, “my lord is righteousness”. He bore the name and fought against the people Yahweh had brought in.

evidence.note: “When אֲדֹנִי־צֶדֶק king of Jerusalem heard that Joshua had taken Ai … and that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel.”
He sends to the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon.
“The five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem …”
Joshua struck them and put them to death.
מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם: the same pattern, the same city.
Salem is Zion: “his covert was in Salem, and his dwelling in Zion.”
Melchizedek, “being translated, king of righteousness (βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης)”: scripture’s own reading of a name built this way, the ‑i taken as joining the two nouns.

note: The name has two words and two roots: אֲדֹנִי from אדנ and צֶדֶק from צדק. BDB’s key a.be.ag is counted by spelling, so the brief’s 68 tokens are nearly all the noun צֶדֶק; the name occurs twice (Jos 10:1, 3). Some take צֶדֶק here as the name of a god; scripture gives no ground for it and the entry does not. The second element is צֶדֶק, in the entry tsedeq.
